question: How does Snowflake achieve resource isolation between an ETL workload and a BI workload on the same data?
options: By running them on separate virtual warehouses that share the same data but have independent compute
By storing two physical copies of the data
By forcing them into a single queue
By converting one workload to row storage
explanation: Separate virtual warehouses give each workload isolated compute over the shared single copy of data, so heavy ETL doesn't starve interactive BI queries.

question: Snowflake's multi-cluster warehouse scaling policy 'Economy' vs 'Standard' differs in that:
options: Standard never adds additional clusters
Economy only works for storage, not compute
Economy adds clusters more conservatively to save credits, potentially allowing more queuing
Standard disables auto-suspend
explanation: The Economy policy favors credit savings by spinning up clusters more conservatively (tolerating some queuing), while Standard prioritizes minimizing queuing/latency.

question: Concurrency scaling in Redshift addresses which problem?
options: Slow single large queries
Query queuing during bursts by transiently adding cluster capacity to run concurrent read queries
High storage costs
Lack of columnar compression
explanation: Redshift concurrency scaling adds transient clusters during read bursts so queued queries run in parallel, then removes them, handling concurrency spikes.

question: Scaling UP (bigger nodes/warehouse size) versus scaling OUT (more clusters/nodes) primarily trades off:
options: Storage durability vs. compression
Security vs. governance
Row vs. columnar storage
Faster individual/large queries (up) vs. more concurrent query throughput (out)
explanation: Scaling up gives more power per query (helps large/complex queries); scaling out adds parallel capacity for many simultaneous queries (helps concurrency).

question: A production dashboard must keep sub-second latency even when a data science team runs heavy exploratory queries on the same tables. The best isolation strategy is:
options: Put both teams on one shared warehouse and hope for the best
Duplicate the tables into two databases and sync them manually
Give each team its own virtual warehouse (or reservation) so compute is isolated over shared data
Disable caching for the data science team
explanation: Dedicated warehouses/reservations isolate compute per workload while sharing one data copy, so heavy exploration can't degrade the latency-sensitive dashboard.
